qs.q:
UNIT 7: THE WORLD OF MASS MEDIA — NGỮ PHÁP & TỪ VỰNG (ĐỀ 1): Mark the letter A, B, C, or D on your answer sheet to indicate the correct answer to each of the following questions.
The viral video spread across social media ______ quickly that millions of people watched it within two hours.
qs.ex: Ngữ pháp Unit 7 Lớp 12 (Adverbial clauses of result): 'so + adv (quickly) + that + S + V'.

qs.q: It was ______ an informative documentary on wildlife conservation that our teacher showed it to the whole grade.
qs.ex: Cấu trúc kết quả với danh từ: 'such + a/an + adj + N + that + S + V'.

qs.q: The online scammer wrote the message ______ he were a bank manager asking for account verification.
qs.ex: Ngữ pháp Unit 7 (Adverbial clauses of manner): 'as if / as though + S + V(quá khứ giả định)'.

qs.q: Digital billboards at busy crossroads use bright animations to attract the ______ of passing drivers.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 7: attract the attention of... = thu hút sự chú ý của...

qs.q: Before sharing breaking news on social networks, responsible netizens always check whether the source is ______.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 7: credible source = nguồn tin đáng tin cậy.

qs.q: There are ______ many advertisements on that free video website that viewers find it annoying to watch films.
qs.ex: Quy tắc đặc biệt: dùng 'so' trước 'many / much / few / little + N + that' (so many advertisements that...).

qs.q: In remote mountain villages, public ______ still broadcast important weather warnings every morning.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 7: public loudspeakers = hệ thống loa phóng thanh công cộng.

qs.q: The AI-generated newsreader spoke ______ naturally that many viewers thought she was a real human presenter.
qs.ex: 'so + adv (naturally) + that...'.

qs.q: Unlike traditional ______ media such as newspapers and magazines, digital media allows readers to leave instant comments.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 7: print media = báo in truyền thống.

qs.q: He talked about the football match ______ he had been in the stadium himself, even though he only watched highlights online.
qs.ex: Mệnh đề chỉ cách thức giả định trái với quá khứ: 'as though / as if + S + had + V3/ed'.

qs.q: The deliberate spread of ______ during natural disasters can cause panic and hinder rescue efforts.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 7: fake news / misinformation = tin giả, thông tin sai lệch.

qs.q: The charity concert received ______ wide publicity in the local press that every seat was sold out.
qs.ex: 'such + adj + N không đếm được (wide publicity) + that...'.

qs.q: Compared with television commercials, placing an advert on a social media platform is much less ______ for small shops.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 7: costly = tốn kém, đắt đỏ.

qs.q: Journalists should report the facts objectively without showing personal ______ towards one side.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 7: bias = sự thiên vị, định kiến.

qs.q: Smartphones have made online news ______ to anyone with an internet connection anytime, anywhere.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 7: accessible to... = có thể tiếp cận được đối với...

qs.q:
Mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best arrangement of utterances or sentences to make a cohesive and coherent exchange or text in each of the following questions from 7 to 11.
**Dear Alex,**
a. At school, our teachers also organise practical projects to help us deliver breaking news quickly and connect communities worldwide.
b. Thank you for your email; it was great to hear about your recent school activities.
c. At weekends, my friends and I join community groups to use mass media critically and responsibly across digital and print media.
d. I’m writing to tell you about how we are learning about digital media, fact-checking misinformation and responsible media use in Unit 7: The World of Mass Media.
e. Write back soon and tell me what your school is doing on this topic!
**Best wishes,**
qs.ex: Trình tự bức thư: Cảm ơn thư trước (b) → Nêu lý do viết thư chia sẻ chủ đề Unit (d) → Kể hoạt động ở trường (a) → Kể hoạt động cuối tuần (c) → Lời kết thư (e): b - d - a - c - e.

qs.q:
a. Nam: Yes, definitely! Let’s sign up together after class today.
b. Mai: Nam, our school club is holding a workshop on digital media, fact-checking misinformation and responsible media use this Saturday. Would you like to join?
c. Mai: Great! I’ll get two registration forms from the club leader.
qs.ex: Trình tự hội thoại 3 lượt: Mai rủ Nam tham gia workshop chủ đề Unit (b) → Nam đồng ý đăng ký (a) → Mai nói sẽ đi lấy phiếu đăng ký (c): b - a - c.

qs.q:
a. To address this, schools and communities are now launching new mass media channels across digital and print media.
b. In the past, many people did not pay enough attention to digital media, fact-checking misinformation and responsible media use.
c. Today, however, both journalists and netizens realise how important it is to use mass media critically and responsibly.
d. As a result, everyone benefits when we work together to help citizens verify credible sources and stop the spread of fake news.
e. These practical programmes help participants deliver breaking news quickly and connect communities worldwide in their daily lives.
qs.ex: Trình tự đoạn văn 5 câu: Thực trạng trước đây (b) → Nhận thức thay đổi ngày nay (c) → Giải pháp triển khai chương trình mới (a) → Tác dụng của các chương trình đó ('These practical programmes') (e) → Kết quả chung (d): b - c - a - e - d.

qs.q:
a. Linh: I’m preparing a poster about digital media, fact-checking misinformation and responsible media use for our English lesson tomorrow.
b. Minh: That sounds interesting! What main benefit are you highlighting on the poster?
c. Minh: Well done, Linh. I’m sure our classmates will learn a lot from your presentation!
d. Linh: I’m focusing on how mass media channels can deliver breaking news quickly and connect communities worldwide and help citizens verify credible sources and stop the spread of fake news.
e. Minh: What are you working on, Linh? You look really focused.
qs.ex: Trình tự hội thoại 5 lượt: Minh hỏi Linh đang làm gì (e) → Linh nói đang làm poster cho bài học tiếng Anh (a) → Minh hỏi lợi ích chính trên poster là gì (b) → Linh giải thích nội dung (d) → Minh khen ngợi (c): e - a - b - d - c.

**PERSPECTIVES ON THE WORLD OF MASS MEDIA**
In recent years, digital media, fact-checking misinformation and responsible media use has attracted growing attention from educators and researchers alike. A recent national survey reports that while over eighty per cent of journalists and netizens recognise the importance of mass media channels, only about thirty-five per cent have <u>**broadcast**</u> these practices into their daily routines across digital and print media. Even when resources are available, many people still struggle to balance their busy schedules with the need to use mass media critically and responsibly.
The challenge lies not only in awareness but also in daily habits. Researchers note that active participants regularly engage in structured tasks that deliver breaking news quickly and connect communities worldwide, whereas passive observers only join occasional events once or twice a year. Consistent practice requires patience and planning, but it delivers lasting rewards. Many individuals simply repeat outdated habits they observed in the past, which prevents them from experiencing how mass media channels can help citizens verify credible sources and stop the spread of fake news.
Fortunately, attitudes are shifting rapidly. **[I]** Most respondents in the survey agreed that everyone should use mass media critically and responsibly, even though many admitted spending less than two hours a week on it themselves. **[II]** Progress was strongest in communities where schools and families worked together as partners. **[III]** Groups can begin by setting clear weekly goals and giving every member a practical role across digital and print media. **[IV]** Small, steady steps like these can turn a difficult challenge into a shared habit of cooperation.
Promoting digital media, fact-checking misinformation and responsible media use matters for the long-term future. Young people who see journalists and netizens model positive behaviours are likely to view these practices as normal, and <u>**they**</u> will carry those values into adulthood. In this way, mass media channels not only deliver breaking news quickly and connect communities worldwide today but also help citizens verify credible sources and stop the spread of fake news for generations to come.
(Adapted from Educational & Social Research Reports – Unit 7: The World of Mass Media)

**PARTNERSHIPS BETWEEN SCHOOLS AND FAMILIES IN UNIT 7: THE WORLD OF MASS MEDIA**
Over the past two years, a research team from the National Institute of Education has tracked 1,500 high school students to evaluate how digital media, fact-checking misinformation and responsible media use affects teenager development. The study found that while nearly ninety per cent of journalists and netizens valued mass media channels, only forty-two per cent <u>**sustained**</u> these routines throughout the entire school year. Students who tried to practise alone often gave up after a few weeks when exam pressure increased.
By contrast, learners whose families and teachers coordinated their guidance achieved far more durable results. In households where parents actively joined weekend activities to use mass media critically and responsibly across digital and print media, teenagers were twice as likely to deliver breaking news quickly and connect communities worldwide. Researchers explained that shared routines reduce the feeling of isolation and turn abstract classroom advice into enjoyable daily habits. Moreover, consistent family involvement helps help citizens verify credible sources and stop the spread of fake news without adding extra stress to students’ timetables.
Schools across the country are now redesigning their programmes based on these findings. **[I]** Instead of assigning theoretical worksheets, teachers invite parents and students to co-sign a simple weekly action plan. **[II]** This joint commitment ensures that classroom lessons are reinforced at home every evening. **[III]** At monthly review sessions, classes celebrate collective progress and exchange practical solutions to common obstacles. **[IV]**
The long-term implications of this partnership model are encouraging. When journalists and netizens work side by side, <u>**they**</u> build mutual respect and lasting life skills. Ultimately, integrating digital media, fact-checking misinformation and responsible media use into both school curricula and family life prepares young citizens to thrive in an increasingly complex world.
(Adapted from National Educational Research Reports – Unit 7: The World of Mass Media)

**WHY CONSISTENCY MATTERS MORE THAN PERFECTION IN UNIT 7: THE WORLD OF MASS MEDIA**
When people first decide to focus on digital media, fact-checking misinformation and responsible media use, they often set overly ambitious targets. Enthusiastic beginners might promise to transform their entire lifestyle in a single weekend, only to feel exhausted a few days later. Studies on habit formation show that well-paced mass media channels are far more effective when built step by step, helping journalists and netizens deliver breaking news quickly and connect communities worldwide without burnout.
The main reason crash campaigns fail is that <u>**they**</u> demand too much willpower at once. <u>**Small, consistent efforts practised every day produce far more lasting results than occasional bursts of intense activity.**</u> When a routine fits naturally into a family’s or student’s daily schedule, it requires less mental strain to maintain.
Experts therefore recommend a <u>**gradual**</u> approach to use mass media critically and responsibly across digital and print media. By starting with one simple task each day and celebrating weekly milestones, learners steadily build momentum. Such steady practice not only strengthens personal discipline but also helps communities help citizens verify credible sources and stop the spread of fake news.
Of course, occasional setbacks are normal during busy exam weeks or family events. Rather than abandoning the goal altogether, resilient learners simply resume their routine the next morning, knowing that patience will <u>**foster**</u> long-term success.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 7: The World of Mass Media)

**COMMUNITY ACTION AND PEER MENTORING IN UNIT 7: THE WORLD OF MASS MEDIA**
Last year, youth unions in three provinces launched a six-month pilot programme to promote digital media, fact-checking misinformation and responsible media use at the grassroots level. Instead of relying on formal lectures, organisers trained two hundred high school volunteers to lead weekend activities where neighbours could use mass media critically and responsibly across digital and print media. Within the first two months, local communities reported <u>**tangible**</u> improvements in daily habits and neighbourhood solidarity.
A key factor behind this success was peer-to-peer mentoring. Teenagers often feel intimidated when adults lecture them, but they respond enthusiastically when classmates demonstrate how mass media channels can deliver breaking news quickly and connect communities worldwide. By working in small teams of five or six, participants shared practical tips, solved everyday problems together and helped one another help citizens verify credible sources and stop the spread of fake news.
Organisers also introduced simple tools to keep momentum high. **[I]** Every participating household received a visual progress board to track weekly milestones. **[II]** Local cultural centres hosted monthly gatherings where teams showcased their most creative ideas. **[III]** These celebrations turned routine tasks into a source of shared pride across the entire district. **[IV]**
Follow-up surveys conducted six months later confirmed that over seventy-five per cent of participants continued practising mass media channels independently. When student volunteers take ownership of community initiatives, <u>**their**</u> enthusiasm inspires both younger children and older residents. The pilot programme demonstrates that youth-led action is one of the most powerful ways to bring the values of Unit 7: The World of Mass Media to life.
(Adapted from Community Development & Youth Studies – Unit 7: The World of Mass Media)

**THE RIPPLE EFFECT OF PEER LEADERSHIP IN UNIT 7: THE WORLD OF MASS MEDIA**
How do positive habits spread across a school or neighbourhood? Sociologists studying digital media, fact-checking misinformation and responsible media use have discovered that peer influence is often stronger than formal rules. When journalists and netizens see their close friends willingly engage in mass media channels, they are far more likely to join in and deliver breaking news quickly and connect communities worldwide.
Nevertheless, launching a new initiative is never without challenges. Organisers note that initial doubts and busy routines are common, and <u>**they**</u> can slow down participation during the first week. <u>**Young people learn most effectively when they observe respected peers applying positive habits in real-life situations.**</u>
For this reason, many schools encourage <u>**voluntary**</u> student ambassadors to lead by example. Whether demonstrating how to use mass media critically and responsibly across digital and print media or sharing practical tips during break time, these role models create a welcoming ripple effect that helps the whole school help citizens verify credible sources and stop the spread of fake news.
Even when a minor <u>**obstacle**</u> arises, a supportive peer group keeps members motivated. What begins as the effort of a few enthusiastic students soon grows into a proud tradition shared by the entire community.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 7: The World of Mass Media)

**OVERCOMING BARRIERS TO DAILY PRACTICE IN UNIT 7: THE WORLD OF MASS MEDIA**
Why do many high school students agree that digital media, fact-checking misinformation and responsible media use is important, yet still find it difficult to use mass media critically and responsibly across digital and print media every day? Educational psychologists point out that modern teenagers face three main barriers: digital distractions, academic pressure and a lack of structured routines. When students feel overwhelmed, they often become <u>**reluctant**</u> to take on new responsibilities at home or in the community.
Fortunately, behavioural research shows that breaking large goals into micro-habits can overcome this hesitation. Instead of trying to change everything overnight, journalists and netizens can start with a fifteen-minute daily routine focused on mass media channels. These manageable actions quickly build confidence and help learners deliver breaking news quickly and connect communities worldwide without interfering with their homework.
Another effective strategy is using a structured weekly checklist. **[I]** When teenagers write down specific times and places for their tasks, they are three times more likely to follow through. **[II]** Sharing <u>**it**</u> with a supportive classmate or family member adds friendly accountability. **[III]** Rather than feeling pressured, students enjoy tracking their streak of completed tasks and seeing how their efforts help citizens verify credible sources and stop the spread of fake news. **[IV]**
Teachers who have introduced micro-habits and checklists into their lessons on Unit 7: The World of Mass Media report remarkable improvements in student engagement. Once young people realise that small daily choices lead to meaningful results, mass media channels stops feeling like a burden and becomes a natural part of who they are.
(Adapted from Adolescent Psychology & Education Review – Unit 7: The World of Mass Media)

**COMBINING TRADITIONAL VALUES WITH MODERN TOOLS IN UNIT 7: THE WORLD OF MASS MEDIA**
In the digital age, some commentators worry that modern technology might distract young people from digital media, fact-checking misinformation and responsible media use. Yet recent educational projects show that when used wisely, digital tools can actually strengthen mass media channels. Shared mobile calendars, reminder apps and online group checklists make it easier than ever for journalists and netizens to deliver breaking news quickly and connect communities worldwide.

**EXPERIENTIAL LEARNING AND THE FUTURE OF UNIT 7: THE WORLD OF MASS MEDIA**
Across Viet Nam, forward-thinking high schools are transforming how students learn about digital media, fact-checking misinformation and responsible media use. Rather than treating Unit 7: The World of Mass Media as a set of vocabulary items to memorise for a test, teachers are integrating experiential learning into every week of the semester. Educators agree that hands-on practice is <u>**indispensable**</u> if young people are to deliver breaking news quickly and connect communities worldwide.
In these classrooms, students work in project teams to investigate real issues and propose ways to use mass media critically and responsibly across digital and print media. For instance, learners might interview local residents, design bilingual awareness posters or organise a school-wide campaign on mass media channels. Through these authentic tasks, journalists and netizens discover how their classroom English connects directly to everyday life.
Assessment methods are evolving alongside teaching styles. **[I]** Instead of relying solely on written quizzes, schools evaluate how effectively students collaborate and apply their plans. **[II]** Each team keeps a reflective portfolio documenting the challenges they faced and how their actions helped help citizens verify credible sources and stop the spread of fake news. **[III]** This approach rewards creativity, persistence and genuine teamwork rather than rote memorisation. **[IV]**
Graduates of experiential programmes consistently report higher confidence when entering university and the workplace. Students <u>**who**</u> have practised solving real-world problems in high school adapt much faster to new environments. By making digital media, fact-checking misinformation and responsible media use an active, lived experience, education equips the next generation with both language proficiency and civic responsibility.
(Adapted from Modern Curriculum & Pedagogy Journal – Unit 7: The World of Mass Media)

**EXPERIENTIAL LEARNING AND THE FUTURE OF UNIT 7: THE WORLD OF MASS MEDIA**
Across Viet Nam, forward-thinking high schools are transforming how students learn about digital media, fact-checking misinformation and responsible media use. Rather than treating Unit 7: The World of Mass Media as a set of vocabulary items to memorise for a test, teachers are integrating experiential learning into every week of the semester. Educators agree that hands-on practice is <u>**indispensable**</u> if young people are to deliver breaking news quickly and connect communities worldwide.
In these classrooms, students work in project teams to investigate real issues and propose ways to use mass media critically and responsibly across digital and print media. For instance, learners might interview local residents, design bilingual awareness posters or organise a school-wide campaign on mass media channels. Through these authentic tasks, journalists and netizens discover how their classroom English connects directly to everyday life.
Assessment methods are evolving alongside teaching styles. **[I]** Instead of relying solely on written quizzes, schools evaluate how effectively students collaborate and apply their plans. **[II]** Each team keeps a reflective portfolio documenting the challenges they faced and how their actions helped help citizens verify credible sources and stop the spread of fake news. **[III]** This approach rewards creativity, persistence and genuine teamwork rather than rote memorisation. **[IV]**
Graduates of experiential programmes consistently report higher confidence when entering university and the workplace. Students <u>**who**</u> have practised solving real-world problems in high school adapt much faster to new environments. By making digital media, fact-checking misinformation and responsible media use an active, lived experience, education equips the next generation with both language proficiency and civic responsibility.
(Adapted from Modern Curriculum & Pedagogy Journal – Unit 7: The World of Mass Media)

**SELF-REFLECTION AND LONG-TERM GROWTH IN UNIT 7: THE WORLD OF MASS MEDIA**
Practising mass media channels is even more rewarding when learners take a few minutes each week to reflect on their progress. Educators studying digital media, fact-checking misinformation and responsible media use have found that students who keep a brief weekly journal understand their own habits much better and find it easier to deliver breaking news quickly and connect communities worldwide.
During busy weeks, people sometimes miss a planned task or make mistakes. Without reflection, <u>**they**</u> may feel discouraged and assume that their efforts have failed. <u>**Honest self-reflection allows learners to turn early mistakes into valuable lessons rather than reasons to give up.**</u>
To make reflection effective, teachers recommend asking <u>**constructive**</u> questions every Sunday evening: What went well when we tried to use mass media critically and responsibly across digital and print media this week, and what small adjustment will help us improve next week?
Over time, this simple habit deepens personal <u>**commitment**</u> and helps journalists and netizens help citizens verify credible sources and stop the spread of fake news with confidence and pride.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 7: The World of Mass Media)

It requires learners to write fifty pages every night.
